title: Latency drop guardrails and action triage - BlueForge
summary: Post-incident handoff focused on a recent 20-30% latency spike related to KV cache TTL mismatch and autoscaler race. Agreed immediate mitigations (circuit breaker, temporary NB cache padding), telemetry gaps to fill, and a plan for a targeted pilot of pre-warming and safer autoscale policy. Follow ups include security signoff for runbook changes and a short benchmark window to validate fix.
topics: autoscale race and cold start behavior
action_items: Daniel Ortiz: Instrument KV cache hit/miss histogram and publish dashboard (due 2026-08-24)
Liam O'Connor: Share draft runbook edits and circuit-breaker config suggestion (due 2026-08-21)
Priya Nair: Approve emergency policy for temporary cache padding and quota adjustments (due 2026-08-22)
Maya Chen: Send pricing-impact estimate for runway if we keep padded capacity for 72 hours (due 2026-08-20)
next_steps: Redwood to provide a short benchmark harness and script for BlueForge to run during their low-traffic window (overnight Thu)
Customer to validate telemetry changes and confirm alarm thresholds in staging
Schedule 30-min follow-up on 2026-08-26 to review pilot metrics and decide on wider rollout
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-08-19
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE); Noah Patel (Redwood CSM); Priya Nair (BlueForge Head of Platform); Daniel Ortiz (BlueForge SRE); Sofia Martinez (BlueForge Product); Ethan Wu (BlueForge Infra)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
Redwood and BlueForge reviewed last night's latency degradation. Root cause appears to be a confluence of TTL misalignment on the KV cache layer and an autoscaler race that produced a wave of cold starts. Immediate mitigations discussed: circuit breaker fallback to smaller model, temporary cache padding, and telemetry augmentation.

---
00:00 Maya (Redwood AE): Okay hi everyone thanks for jumping on, we wanted to run through what we learned from the incident overnight and make sure the handoff is clear, we have Liam and Noah from our side, and then Priya, Daniel, Sofia on the BlueForge side. Can folks hear me?
00:12 Priya (BlueForge): Yes loud and clear, thanks Maya. Appreciate you pulling this together.
00:17 Daniel (BlueForge SRE): Morning — well afternoon — yeah we looked at traces, it's messy but we do have an initial timeline.
00:25 Liam (Redwood SE): I'll try not to drown in logs but I'll walk through the sequence we saw on the call. I have a quick slide link in the chat — link: https://redwood.app/notes/blueforge-aug19 (internal)
00:40 Maya: Cool. Quick ask — we'll keep this to action-oriented items. We want to make sure we don't miss policy/approval steps.
00:48 Priya: Sure. We're mainly trying to understand the incidence vector and what we need to change in our autoscale policies / runbooks.
01:02 Daniel: Timeline we observed: at 02:14 UTC we saw a step increase in 95th percentile latency, about 20–30% above baseline, lasting ~18 minutes with small oscillations after. Across services the traces correlate to inference endpoints queuing and then large KV cache miss ratios.
01:23 Liam: Right, our trace overlays with your traces — the pattern suggests a TTL mismatch. BlueForge's client TTL for prefix caching is 45s while the server-side TTL default changed to 30s after a config push last week; that creates a short window where clients send a prefix expecting fresh cache, but the server evicted and needs to re-cache with a cold path.
01:45 Sofia (BlueForge Product): Wait, so the client kept using a cached key that no longer existed? That seems like a coordination bug - how does the platform normally avoid that?
01:55 Noah (Redwood CSM): Typically we align TTLs for the hot prefixes and we have a grace period; looks like the grace period wasn't in effect because the backend TTL override rolled earlier than expected.
02:09 Ethan (BlueForge): On top of that we had the autoscaler thresholds set to 60% CPU, and when the cache misses happened we suddenly had more long tail token processing and the pool started to spin up new pods — there's an autoscaler race where multiple pods boot and hit cold model loads simultaneously. That's the cold-start multiplier.
02:28 Liam: Exactly, so two compounding issues: cache churn + autoscaler race. The cold loads amplify latency and cause further queuing, creating the spike.
02:37 Daniel: We also saw a number of 429s and some queued requests with long token times.
02:44 Priya: What about fallback / circuit-breakers? I thought we had a fallback path to a smaller model or older pinned model.
02:52 Maya: We do, but the fallback threshold was not reached due to mis-tagged error codes — some of the evictions manifest as 200s with slow response rather than explicit errors, so the circuit didn't trip.
03:05 Daniel: Ah yes, our logs showed successful responses but with 6–7x latency for certain tokens. So the heuristic didn't trigger.
03:12 Liam: We recommended in earlier runbooks using response-time based circuit heuristics in addition to error-count based ones. Looks like that wasn't enabled in this environment.
03:22 Priya: That's an operational gap. What do you recommend immediately?
03:27 Liam: Short term: enable a response-time circuit breaker — e.g., if P95 > 2x baseline for 3 consecutive one-minute windows, route to fallback model for the next 10 minutes. Also add a temporary "cache padding" where we hold some reserved capacity (pre-warmed instances or padded tokens) for 72 hours until TTLs are reconciled.
03:48 Maya: We'll also share a suggested circuit config and a one-page runbook patch for emergency apply. Liam will draft.
03:55 Noah: And we'll propose a safe autoscale policy: prefer gradual scale steps (25% increments) with ramp window to avoid simultaneous cold starts; plus a pre-warm hook so model artifacts load before traffic is sent.
04:12 Ethan: Pre-warm hook sounds useful — but that requires infra changes. How heavy is that?
04:17 Liam: Not huge — we can add a lifecycle hook that requests model weights load during scale events. There's an existing API in Redwood's Dedicated runtime; we can provide a small script to call it as part of the autoscaler lifecycle.
04:30 Priya: OK. For the runbook changes we'll need security review — any changes to fallback or pre-warm would need sign off.
04:37 Maya: Noted — add that to action items. Noah will work with Priya to coordinate the review.
04:44 Daniel: Telemetry gaps — we need better instrumentation between the KV layer and inference nodes. Right now we have a generic cache hit metric but not a per-prefix hit/miss histogram and not correlation to model cold-start events.
05:01 Liam: Agree. Action: instrument per-prefix KV hit/miss, and emit a combined event when cache miss coincides with model load duration > threshold. That will help us trigger automated mitigations.
05:15 Priya: Also alarms — we had an alarm on 95th but it fired late; maybe silence thresholds need lowering or smoothing.
05:22 Noah: We'll recommend lowering the alarm to 1.5x baseline for 2 consecutive windows, and add an alert playbook that suggests applying the circuit-breaker patch automatically in non-prod and manual approval in prod.
05:35 Sofia: On the business side, product wants to understand user impact and SLA risk — Daniel any numbers?
05:41 Daniel: We saw error budget consumption at roughly 0.3% additional latency impact on daily p95 for the service. For correlated downstream services the impact was noticeable. We have a spreadsheet I'll share.
05:52 Maya: Great. Can we get that shared doc? Put in the notes.
06:00 Daniel: I'll upload to the incident folder — link posted in chat.
06:05 Liam: One technical nuance — the eviction TTL change was a config push with an automated migration that didn't include a coordinated client push. We should look at adding a gate to config changes that affect client-visible TTL or default behaviors.
06:19 Priya: We do have a change advisory but it didn't flag this because the change was in a templated infra module. We'll add a pre-deploy validation to catch mismatched TTLs going forward.
06:30 Noah: Another mitigation is to make client-side TTLs resilient: have clients respect server-supplied TTLs and fallback to short caches rather than long. That avoids client optimism.
06:40 Ethan: That requires an SDK change — we can do a quick client-opt-in patch for the languages we support.
06:46 Lily (Redwood SE) - note: Lily not present; avoid adding.
06:48 Priya: Okay let's triage what we do immediately vs medium-term. Immediate: response-time circuit + temporary cache padding + telemetry instrument. Medium: pre-warm hooks + gradual autoscale + SDK TTL respect. Long: change-gate for TTLs, runbook automation and chaos test coverage.
07:05 Maya: Works for us. We'll treat the immediate triage as hotfixes. Liam will draft configs; Daniel will run instrumentation tests in staging tonight. Priya you'll approve the policy.
07:16 Daniel: Quick question — is there any recommended threshold for the padding? Like how many nodes to keep warm?
07:21 Liam: Start with 10% of baseline QPS capacity or a fixed minimum of 2 pre-warmed pods for each hot shard, whichever is greater. We'll provide a calculator.
07:32 Priya: Ok that seems reasonable. I'll need to understand cost impact.
07:35 Maya: I'll send a short estimate of cost delta for 72-hour padding window.
07:40 Sofia: On the customer comms side, we'll prepare a short note to customers. Need to confirm if we classify this as scheduled planned change or incident — probably incident.
07:48 Noah: Yes treat as incident, and we'll provide a brief post-incident summary after the follow-up.
07:52 Ethan: One more infra note: some of our nodes use an older image that takes longer to load models; we should set image minimums or a blacklist.
07:59 Liam: Good catch. Add image start-time to our telemetry so we can correlate boot time to cold load durations.
08:07 Daniel: I'll add that metric.
08:12 Priya: Sounds like we have clear owners. Anything else?
08:18 Maya: We'll recap next steps — send runbook patch, telemetry changes, benchmark harness. Schedule follow up for Aug 26.
08:26 Sofia: Can we also get a small A/B of the circuit-change in staging vs prod? We'd like to see behavioral differences.
08:33 Liam: Absolutely, we can help run a 4-hour window of simulated load to validate. We'll coordinate.
08:39 Priya: Cool. Thanks everyone, appreciate the fast response.
08:44 Maya: Thanks all. We'll email notes and action items.

Questions (auto):
- Should circuit-breaker be error-count or response-time based? (Answer: both; response-time based recommended in this case)
- How long to keep temporary padding? (Answer: 72 hours or until TTLs reconciled and pilot validated)
